name: Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir
drug_class: SARS-CoV-2 main protease (3CL protease) inhibitor, boosted with ritonavir (CYP3A inhibitor)
route_note: co-packaged oral tablets taken twice daily for 5 days, started within 5 days of symptoms

discovery.note: Designed in 2020 from Pfizer's earlier SARS-CoV-1 protease inhibitor lufotrelvir as an orally available covalent nitrile inhibitor.

tagline: Oral COVID-19 antiviral pairing a protease blocker with a ritonavir booster
summary: Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir is an oral COVID-19 treatment that combines nirmatrelvir, an inhibitor of the SARS-CoV-2 main protease, with low-dose ritonavir to slow its breakdown. In unvaccinated high-risk adults it cut hospitalisation or death by about 89% when started early. Its many drug interactions through CYP3A inhibition are a major practical issue.
mechanism: SARS-CoV-2 translates its genome into long polyproteins that the main protease (Mpro, also called 3C-like protease) must cut into functional replication proteins. Nirmatrelvir is a peptidomimetic whose nitrile warhead forms a reversible covalent bond with the catalytic cysteine (Cys145) of Mpro, stopping polyprotein processing and viral replication.

Nirmatrelvir is rapidly metabolised by CYP3A4. Ritonavir, an HIV protease inhibitor used here at a low dose, strongly inhibits CYP3A4 and raises nirmatrelvir concentrations, but it also raises levels of many other CYP3A-cleared drugs.
uses: Mild to moderate COVID-19 in adults at high risk of progression to severe disease
Mild to moderate COVID-19 in high-risk adolescents aged 12 years and older weighing at least 40 kg (US emergency use)

history.title: Design
history.detail: Pfizer chemists design PF-07321332 and begin a fast-tracked development programme.

history.title: EPIC-HR
history.detail: Interim results show about 89% reduction in COVID-19 hospitalisation or death among high-risk unvaccinated adults treated within 3 days.

history.title: Emergency use
history.detail: The FDA issues an emergency use authorisation on 22 December 2021; the UK approves it on 31 December.

history.title: EU and WHO
history.detail: The EU grants conditional authorisation in January 2022; WHO strongly recommends it for high-risk non-severe patients in April 2022.

history.title: Rebound
history.detail: Reports of symptom and viral rebound after treatment draw attention; studies find rebound also occurs without treatment.

history.title: Full FDA approval
history.detail: The FDA approves Paxlovid for high-risk adults on 25 May 2023.

history.title: Long COVID trials
history.detail: Randomised trials (including STOP-PASC) find no clear benefit of extended courses for long COVID.

pk.half_life: nirmatrelvir about 6 h when boosted with ritonavir
pk.bioavailability: not determined; food has little effect
pk.metabolism: nirmatrelvir by CYP3A4 (largely blocked by ritonavir); ritonavir by CYP3A4 and CYP2D6
pk.excretion: nirmatrelvir mainly renal when boosted; ritonavir mainly faeces

serious: serious drug–drug interactions via CYP3A inhibition
hypersensitivity reactions, including toxic epidermal necrolysis and Stevens–Johnson syndrome (rare)
risk of HIV-1 protease inhibitor resistance in uncontrolled or undiagnosed HIV
safety.boxed_warning: Significant drug interactions: co-administration with certain CYP3A-dependent or CYP3A-inducing drugs may cause serious or life-threatening reactions or loss of virological response (US label).

facts: Paxlovid went from first synthesis to emergency authorisation in under two years.
Dose reduction is needed in moderate renal impairment, and it is not recommended in severe renal impairment in many labels.
A bitter or metallic taste ('Paxlovid mouth') is one of the commonest side effects.

references.title: Hammond J et al. Oral nirmatrelvir for high-risk, nonhospitalized adults with Covid-19. NEJM 2022
